claims.claim: Gen 10 is a list of the peoples descended from Noah's three sons, structured by son — Japheth vv. 2–5, Ham vv. 6–20, Shem vv. 21–31 — with a closing summary (v. 32).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 10, read in full.

claims.claim: The Table's organising criteria are descent, land, language, and clan: the refrains "after their families, after their tongues, in their lands, after their nations" (vv. 5, 20, 31) and "according to their generations, in their nations" (v. 32).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 10, read in full; Speiser, Comment (P's catalogue of states; criteria of country, language, ethnic affinities).

claims.claim: The names in the Table are predominantly eponymous or geographical rather than personal individuals; many are plural or gentilic forms.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 188–223 (names are eponymous; geographical principle); Speiser, Note x 2 (the list includes outright ethnic names, e.g. Kittim, Rodanim, which are plurals); Westermann.

claims.claim: The Table is a composite of P and J material: P provides the framework, with J insertions (notably the Nimrod piece vv. 8–12 and the Canaanite list vv. 15–19). The outline is agreed; the exact verse assignments differ between scholars.
claims.evidence: Skinner (P: 1a, 2–5, 6–7, 20, 21–24?, 29–32; J: 8–12, 13–14, 15–19, 21, 25–30); Ryle (P: 1, 2–5, 6–7, 20, 22–31; J: 8–19, 21); Westermann (R on P's system with two J insertions, 10:8–19 and 10:24–30). The disagreement on 10:21–24 is the reason for Probable, not Established.

claims.claim: The Table's geography follows a directional principle: Japheth to the north and west (coastlands, Anatolia, the Aegean), Ham to the south (Africa and the southern Levant), Shem to the east (Mesopotamia, Arabia) — not colour, language, or race.
claims.evidence: Skinner (geographical principle; "not colour, language, or race"); Speiser, Notes x 2–6 (Japheth: Anatolia, Aegean, and beyond; criterion geographic).

claims.claim: The Table does not state a "three sons, three continents" scheme; that reading is later.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 10, read in full (no continental scheme stated); NS dossier §4.3 (Haynes) — the finding that the reading is late, noted here not re-researched; Jubilees 8 gives the earliest elaborated form (clm-nb-061).

claims.claim: Nimrod (10:8–12) is the only figure in the Table given a biographical narrative rather than a bare name: Cush's son, a gibbôr and "mighty hunter before the LORD", whose kingdom began at Babel, Erech, Accad (and Calneh) and extended to Assyria (Nineveh, Rehoboth, Calah, Resen).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 10:8–12, read in full; Speiser, Note x 8–12 ("these five verses constitute a fragment from, or a summary of, an account dealing with the exploits of Nimrod").

claims.claim: "Before the LORD" (lipnê YHWH, 10:9) is ambiguous: it is read as "in defiance / against" (LXX enantion, Josephus, Targums, K&D, Clarke, Augustine, Philo) or as merely descriptive of magnitude or divine favour (Ryle; Speiser "by the will of Yahweh").
claims.evidence: K&D (defiance); Clarke (rebel); Augustine CD 16.4 (enantion = both "before" and "against"); Ryle (merely descriptive of magnitude, cf. Gen 23:6, Jonah 3:3); Speiser, Note x 9 ("by the will of Yahweh"). See §8.2.

claims.claim: Nimrod has not been identified with any historically attested Mesopotamian king or god. Proposed identifications — Gilgamesh (nearest analogy), the Kassite king Nazi-Marutta/Nazi-maraddash, the god Ninurta, Tukulti-Ninurta I via Ninus — are all unproven.
claims.evidence: BDB H5248 ("etymology and meaning wholly unknown"; Nazi-maraddash "but dubious"); Skinner ("no convincing Assyriological prototype; Gilgamesh nearest analogy"); Speiser, Comment (Tukulti-Ninurta I chain — his argument, not consensus); ISBE via BibleHub Topical Bible ("not identified... quite unlikely" for the Kassite king). See §8.1.

claims.claim: Cush in Gen 10 denotes two distinct regions whose names coincide: Ethiopia (10:6–7) and the Kassite land Cossaea (10:8; cf. Gen 2:13).
claims.evidence: Speiser, Note x 6 (two widely separated lands, "by coincidence"); Skinner (Kush possibly the Kassites in the Nimrod passage); Gunkel (R conflated Kush = Ethiopia in P with Kassū in J).

claims.claim: The four Mesopotamian cities of 10:10 (Babel, Erech, Accad, Calneh) and the four Assyrian cities of 10:11–12 (Nineveh, Rehoboth, Calah, Resen) reflect genuine historical geography: Babel = Babylon, Erech = Uruk, Nineveh and Calah are known Assyrian capitals. Calneh is unidentified, and Speiser's repointing of "Calneh" to kullānāh ("all of them") is a proposal, not an established reading.
claims.evidence: Skinner (Babel = Bab-ili; Erech = Uruk; Akkad site uncertain; Calneh undiscovered; Assyrian cities derived from Babylonia); Speiser, Note x 10 (repointing, with Albright JNES 3 [1944] 254f.; Accad's mention "points up the soundness of the source"); K&D (the four Assyrian cities form one composite great city = Nineveh).

claims.claim: The Philistines are traced to the Casluhim (10:14), with a Caphtor connection (Amos 9:7; Jer 47:4) reconciled as a Casluhian colony strengthened by Caphtor immigrants.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 10:14, read in full; K&D (Casluchian colony strengthened by Caphtor immigrants); Ryle (Philistines relatives of the Egyptians per J); Speiser, Comment (J identifies Japheth with the Philistines; P does not mention them).

claims.claim: The Canaanites' listing under Ham (10:15–19) rests on geographic and political association, not linguistic kinship: Canaanite is closely related to Hebrew.
claims.evidence: Speiser, Note x 6 ("the subsuming of Canaan under Hamites appears at first to be strange. The solution is to be sought apparently in geographic and political connection rather than in ethnolinguistic relations"); Skinner (Canaanites incl. the Hittites problem, vv. 16–18b likely a gloss).

claims.claim: The Table omits the Babylonians as a named people and omits Peleg's descendants (except the notice in 10:25). The omissions are best explained by source history — the Babylonians once entered under Mesopotamian Cush; Peleg's line reserved for P's Gen 11 genealogy — but both explanations are hypotheses.
claims.evidence: Skinner (Babylonians omitted in P "unexplained"); Speiser, Comment (Babylonian entry once under Mesopotamian Cush, dating the verses to no later than the end of the Kassite period; Peleg's descendants left out in favour of P's parallel genealogy xi 18–27).

claims.claim: The number 70 for the nations is not stated in the text; counting the names yields different totals depending on method (Jewish 70, Fathers 72, Augustine 73 "or rather 72").
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 10, read in full (no total given); K&D ("the number 70 is nowhere given or hinted at"; Jewish Midrash 70: 14/31/25; Rabbis 14/30/26; Fathers 72); Gunkel (70 Jewish / 72 Christian); Augustine CD 16.3, 16.6, 16.11 (73 counted, "or rather... 72 nations").

claims.claim: Peleg's name is explained in 10:25 by "in his days was the earth divided" (niplĕgâ, Niph'al of pālag H6385, "split, divide").
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 10:25, read in full; BDB pālag H6385 (Niph'al Perfect 3fs niplĕgâ Gen 10:25).

claims.claim: The Table presupposes the dispersion (10:18 "the families of the Canaanites spread abroad"; 10:32 "by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood") while Gen 11:1–9 narrates the dispersion as a later event. The narrative order is retrospective, not strictly chronological.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 10:18, 32; 11:1–9, read in full; Augustine CD 16.15 (the narrative "goes back to gather up what it had passed over"); Skinner (the Tower section is "independent of and irreconcilable with ch. 10" in narrative order).

claims.claim: The Table's horizon reflects first-millennium geographical knowledge: P's Japheth list is not later than the 7th century BC (known to Jeremiah and Ezekiel), and much of the same information is too late for J's times.
claims.evidence: Skinner (P pre-exilic; terminus a quo 8th c., Cimmerians/Scythians; Persians/Arabs absent); Speiser, Comment (Japhethite group as recorded by P "not later than the seventh century B.C., since it was known to Jeremiah and Ezekiel").

claims.claim: Gen 11:1–9 narrates a single episode in three linked motifs: the building of a city and tower, the confusion of languages, and the dispersion of humanity.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:1–9, read in full; Westermann (three motifs amalgamated, originally independent; dispersion already in 9:18–19, 10:25; confusion only in 11:1–9).

claims.claim: The builders' stated purposes are to make a name for themselves and to avoid being scattered (11:4); the text states no flood-refuge motive.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:4, read in full. The flood-refuge motive is Josephus's addition (Ant. 1.4.2), rejected by Calvin — see clm-nb-065.

claims.claim: The building materials (brick for stone, bitumen for mortar, 11:3) are Babylonian, not Palestinian: the passage's local colour is Mesopotamian.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:3, read in full; Gunkel (brick-and-bitumen vs Palestinian stone — "Palestinian puzzled by finest buildings of worst material"); Ryle (the writer is more familiar with stone-and-mortar building than brick-and-bitumen — Israelite origin; ḥēmār here, Gen 14:10, Ex 2:3); Speiser (in a normal Hebrew context the reference "would be out of place and confusing").

claims.claim: The tower's "top in heaven" (11:4, literally "head in the sky") echoes the Esagila tradition: Enuma Elish VI 60–62, "They raised the head of Esagila toward Apsu", Esagila meaning "the structure with upraised head". This is Speiser's argument for a literary (cuneiform) source for the story.
claims.evidence: Speiser, Comment pp. 75–76 (read directly; Orientalia 25 [1956] 317–23); Enuma Elish VI entry `source-enuma-elish-tablet-vi` (verified, PR #203). The connection is Speiser's reading of VI 60–62; the dossier does not independently verify the Akkadian.

claims.claim: The story is an etiology: it explains the present diversity of languages, the dispersion of peoples, and the name Babel.
claims.evidence: Westermann (narrative is etiological — present situation explained by primeval event); Gunkel, Skinner (etiological function agreed). Whether it is *only* etiology is debated — see DQ-15, §3.5.

claims.claim: No Babylonian version of the Tower story has been discovered; the K 3657 fragment once cited contains nothing of the sort.
claims.evidence: Skinner p. 224–231 ("no Babylonian version of the story discovered (K 3657 fragment shown to contain nothing of the sort)"); Ryle ("No trace of this narrative has with any certainty... been discovered in the cuneiform inscriptions").

claims.claim: The nearest ANE parallel is the Sumerian Spell of Nudimmud (Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta 134–155): Enki changes the speech in human mouths. But the passage has no tower, no city-building, no dispersion, and no punishment, and its direction is disputed — Kramer read it backward-looking (Enki confounded a once-unified speech), Alster/Vanstiphout forward-looking (an incantation hoping for future unity).
claims.evidence: ETCSL c.1.8.2.3 lines 134–155, read directly; Westermann (Kramer JAOS 63 [1943] 191–193; JAOS 88 [1968] 108–111 — Kramer second-hand via Westermann; the Alster/Vanstiphout reading second-hand via a 2026 essay). The ETCSL text as it stands reads forward-looking.

claims.claim: The story's structure has been analysed as two recensions (Gunkel: city recension vs tower recension) or as a unity with gradual pre-literary growth (Westermann, Cassuto). Skinner judges Gunkel plausible, with the duplicate ending as the weak point.
claims.evidence: Gunkel pp. 93–100 (full two-recension analysis); Westermann (Gunkel's split "dismembers vv. 4–5"; unity favoured); Skinner (Gunkel plausible, weak point the duplicate ending). See §8.3.

claims.claim: "Babel" (11:9) is explained in the text by folk etymology from bālal "to confuse, mix"; the historical etymology is Bab-ilu/Bab-ili "gate of God".
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:9, read in full; BDB bālal H1101 (sense 1 "mingle, confuse", Gen 11:7, 9); Skinner, Ryle, Dummelow (Bab-ilu "gate of God" — Dummelow second-hand via search, see §12.1); K&D (bālal "according to divine direction... as a standing memorial").

claims.claim: God "came down" twice (11:5, 7): an anthropomorphic judicial inspection followed by judicial infliction. Whether the double descent reflects two tradition layers (Westermann) or a recapitulation (Augustine CD 16.5) is unresolved.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:5, 7, read in full (the double descent is Established from the text); Westermann (two tradition layers); Augustine CD 16.5 ("Let us go down" as recapitulation explaining the descent); K&D (judicial cognizance, then judicial infliction).

claims.claim: "Let us go down" (11:7) is a plural of deliberation. Explanations include the divine council or heavenly court (Gunkel: remnant of a polytheistic Vorlage; Ryle: Jehovah addressing the powers of heaven), the plural of majesty (Speiser), and the angels (Augustine CD 16.5–6, who also weighs the Trinity for Gen 1:26 but prefers the angels here).
claims.evidence: Speiser, Note xi 7 (plural of majesty; celestial staff); Gunkel (divine-council remnant); Ryle ("sons of Elohim", cf. Job 1:6); Augustine CD 16.5–6 (angels as fellow-labourers). See §3.2.

claims.claim: The confusion of tongues is presented in the text as a divine judgement on human pride, not as a natural linguistic development; the punishment fits the offence (the tongue as the instrument of domination — Augustine CD 16.4).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:5–9, read in full (the text's own presentation); Augustine CD 16.4 ("As the tongue is the instrument of domination, in it pride was punished; so that man, who would not understand God when He issued His commands, should be misunderstood when he himself gave orders"). The historical-linguistic question is separate — see DQ-15.

claims.claim: Etemenanki, the ziggurat of Marduk at Babylon ("House of the foundation of heaven and earth"), is the best candidate for the building that inspired the story: it stood in the city the story names, was rebuilt on a colossal scale (base ~91 m square, height 180 cubits per the Esagil tablet) when Judeans were living in Babylonia, and its builders described it in the same words ("make its top equal to heaven"). The identification is not proven — no text links the two directly.
claims.evidence: George, CUSAS 17 (read directly: dimensions, history, the Nebuchadnezzar inscriptions); Skinner (E-temen-an-ki as candidate; Nabopolassar "make its top equal to heaven"; same phrase in Nebuchadnezzar); theartnewbie summary second-hand for "best candidate by far" (not cited as evidence). Speiser's chronological objection is recorded in §8.7.

claims.claim: The Nebuchadnezzar II stele (Schøyen MS 2063, CUSAS 17) depicts the king before Etemenanki and records the mobilisation of "all countries everywhere, each and every population" as corvée labour for the ziggurat — a tower built by many nations.
claims.evidence: George, CUSAS 17 ch. VII (read directly: stele 47 × 25 cm, black basalt; epigraph "E-temen-anki, the ziqqurrat of Babylon"; inscription an abridgement of Nbk no. 17; appendix translation of the mobilisation passage, ll. 62–132).

claims.claim: The E-sangil Tablet's figures (base 180 cubits ≈ 90–91 m; seven stages) are idealised mathematical exercises, not an eyewitness description; no firm consensus exists on whether the tower had seven or eight stages.
claims.evidence: George, CUSAS 17 (read directly: "It is a compilation of mathematical exercises and very probably draws its figures from an ideal, not from reality... No firm consensus has emerged over the number of stages (seven or eight)").

claims.claim: The tower's identification with E-zida at Borsippa (Birs Nimrud, 153 ft) rests on local and Jewish tradition, not on the biblical text; K&D leaves the connection uncertain.
claims.evidence: Skinner (E-zida at Borsippa, Birs Nimrud, local/Jewish tradition = the tower; the 153 ft figure is second-hand via the Bullinger/Chesney summary, see §6.3); Ryle (Borsippa/Birs Nimrud = temple of Bel-Nebo, seven tiers = seven planets); K&D (Birs Nimrud connection "must remain, at least for the present, a matter of uncertainty").

claims.claim: The builders' project is presented in reception as impious pride (Augustine: "erected this tower against the Lord"; the safe way to heaven is humility) and as folly (Speiser: the narrator's criticism of man's folly and presumption). The text itself does not name the sin explicitly.
claims.evidence: Augustine CD 16.4 (read directly); Speiser, Comment (read directly: the narrator "employed these data solely as a basis for his criticism of man's folly and presumption"). Traditional because it is a reading of the text's implication, not a statement of the text.

claims.claim: Pentecost (Acts 2:5–11) is the New Testament converse of Babel: the scattering of one language is reversed by the gathering of many languages (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 41 §16; Augustine, Sermon 271).
claims.evidence: Acts 2:5–11 (KJV, the text itself — see conn-nb-024); Gregory of Nazianzus Oration 41 §16 and Augustine Sermon 271 second-hand via secondary summaries (not read directly — see §12.4). The patristic reading is Traditional; the Acts text is Established.

claims.claim: Gen 11:10–26 is P's genealogy from Shem to Terah, resuming the tôlĕḏôt pattern of Gen 5 but with nine (MT) rather than ten members, and without the total life-span and "then he died" formulae.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:10–26, read in full; Westermann (same scheme as Gen 5 minus total life-span and "then he died"); Skinner (P; 9 generations MT); Speiser (resumes the genealogical record interrupted at the end of ch. 5).

claims.claim: The MT gives nine generations Shem→Terah; the LXX inserts Cainan (Kainam) between Arpachshad and Shelah with Shelah's figures, making ten; 1 Chr 1:24 omits Cainan.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:10–26, read in full; Skinner (LXX inserts Cainan, duplicates Shelah's figures; secondary); Westermann (9 members, not 10); Ryle (Cainan inserted by LXX before Shelah, figures identical to Shelah's — suspicious; omitted in 1 Chr 1:24); Jubilees 8:1–3 (Kainam, read directly).

claims.claim: The begetting-age sums differ systematically: MT 390, Sam 1040, LXX 1270 (LXX-A 1170). The Flood-to-Abraham totals are MT 290, Sam 940, LXX 1070 (Ryle) or 1170 (Skinner), Jubilees 567. The LXX discrepancy turns on the handling of Cainan and the "two years" offset and is not resolved in this dossier.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 231–234 (chronology table: MT 290, Sam 940, LXX 1170, Jubilees 567; begetting sums MT 390, Sam 1040, LXX 1270, LXX-A 1170); Ryle (MT 290, LXX 1070, Sam 940, Jubilees 567; begetting-age adjustments tabulated). Both tables read directly; the discrepancy is reported, not resolved.

claims.claim: The ages are schematic, not a dependable historical record: MT shows levelling (Shem exactly 100 at Arpachshad's birth and 500 years after; Arpachshad and Shelah both 403 years after their first sons; Shelah, Peleg, and Serug each 30 at their first sons).
claims.evidence: Speiser, Comment pp. 79–80 (read directly: "MT is transparently schematic... a certain amount of leveling... If any particular system of computation was employed... its nature is no longer apparent"); Skinner (Bosse's systems noted without endorsement); Westermann (Sam/LXX inflation as scribal theology).

claims.claim: "Two years after the flood" (11:10) is judged a gloss by Skinner, Westermann, Dillmann, Budde, and Holzinger, but the lectio difficilior argues for keeping it (Westermann, Gunkel); B. Jacob reconciles it (Noah began to beget at 500 in the year of the flood).
claims.evidence: Skinner (gloss, to start a new era with Arpachshad); Westermann (gloss per Dillmann/Budde/Holzinger/Skinner, but lectio difficilior argues for keeping it); Gunkel (P's approximate reckoning, do not emend); B. Jacob via Westermann. See §7.2.

claims.claim: The lifespan decline after the Flood (Shem 600 → Nahor 148) is a feature of the text. K&D's causal explanation (the Flood changed the climate; the separation changed men's habits) is interpretation, not established fact.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:10–26, read in full (the decline itself); K&D (the causal attribution — read directly, and labelled here as K&D's interpretation); Ryle ("in the approach to historic times the figures become more normal"); Josephus Ant. 1.6.5 (life diminished by degrees until Moses, then 120 years).

claims.claim: Arpachshad appears as the third son of Shem in 10:22 (a people/land) but as the eldest son and a person in 11:10 — two traditions P did not reconcile.
claims.evidence: Skinner (Arpachshad 10:22 third son vs 11:10 eldest — different traditions); Westermann (Arpachshad in 10:22 people/land, third son, vs 11:10 person, eldest — different traditions, not two individuals); Gunkel (same); Speiser, Note xi 10 (Arpachshad third of Shem's five sons per x 22; his branch now singled out).

claims.claim: The names Serug and Nahor correspond to known Mesopotamian toponyms in the Harran region (Sarug; Nahur in the Mari documents), suggesting very old traditions behind the genealogy.
claims.evidence: Speiser, Notes xi 20, 22 + Comment (Sarug in the region of Harran, Driver p. 139; Nahur in the Mari documents, ARM XV p. 130; population of Nahur in Mari times included West Semitic elements; "borrowings from names of places are... a well-known and universal practice"); Ryle (Serug: town/region near Harran; Nahor: name found in early Assyrian business documents).

claims.claim: The genealogy's function is transitional: it bridges the primeval history to the patriarchal history, narrowing from all humanity (Gen 5) to one branch toward Abraham.
claims.evidence: Westermann (not a continuation of Gen 5 — Gen 5 = whole humanity, 11:10–26 = one branch toward Abraham; P marks the transition by omitting the tenth); Skinner; Speiser, Comment (the record resumes and narrows to the line to which Abraham belonged).

claims.claim: The nine-vs-ten question: P marks the transition to patriarchal history by omitting the tenth member (Westermann), or Noah/Abraham counts as the tenth (Gunkel); the LXX supplies Cainan to make ten.
claims.evidence: Westermann (9 members, not 10 — P marks the transition by omitting the tenth); Gunkel (9 members, Noah or Abraham as the tenth); Skinner (9 MT, 10 LXX with Cainan). See §7.2.

claims.claim: Gen 11:27–32 (Terah's tôlĕḏôt) is composite: P (vv. 27, 31, 32) with a J insert (vv. 28–30). Haran dies in Ur of the Chaldees, Sarai is barren, Terah leads Abram, Lot, and Sarai from Ur toward Canaan, settles in Harran, and dies there at 205.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:27–32, read in full; Skinner (P: 27, 31, 32; J: 28–30); Gunkel (P = vv. 27, 31, 32; vv. 28–30 J); Speiser (xi 10–27, 31–32: P; 28–30: J).

claims.claim: "Ur of the Chaldees" (11:28, 31; 15:7) is given by both J and P, so the problem antedates the LXX by centuries; the LXX's "land" for "Ur" does not solve the Chaldean anachronism.
claims.evidence: Speiser, Note xi 28 (LXX "land" suggests Heb. ʾereṣ for ʾûr, but the variant could have been influenced by "land" in the preceding phrase; "the place name is given by J, as well as P (31), so that the problem involved antedates LXX by many centuries"); Ryle ("in Ur of the Chaldees" possibly a gloss added by a later hand, as in 15:7).

claims.claim: The location of Ur is disputed: southern Ur (Tell el-Mukayyar, S. Babylonia, seat of moon-god Sin) per Skinner and Ryle, vs northern Ur (Urfa/Edessa, or Ammian's "Ur nomine persicum castellum") per K&D and JFB.
claims.evidence: Skinner/Ryle (Uru = Tell el-Mukayyar, >100 miles SE of Babylon, principal seat of moon-god Sin); K&D (Ammian's "Ur nomine persicum castellum" between Hatra and Nisibis, or Orhoi/Edessa = Urfa); JFB (Ur = now Orfa/Edessa, "light"/"fire", fire-worship). See §7.4, DQ-01.

claims.claim: The Chaldeans are late arrivals in Mesopotamia (not datable before the end of the second millennium) and the name does not appear in inscriptions until long after Abram's time; "Ur of the Chaldees" is therefore anachronistic for a second-millennium Abram.
claims.evidence: Speiser, Comment (Chaldeans late arrivals, "could not possibly be dated before the end of the second millennium"; Aramaeans not automatically placeable in the patriarchal period; "even if one were to follow LXX in reading 'land' for 'Ur,' the anachronism of the Chaldeans would remain unsolved"); Ryle (Chaldeans predominant 7th c. BC; name does not appear in inscriptions until long after Abram's time).

claims.claim: The one fact beyond serious dispute is that the patriarchs' home was in the district of Harran, not at Ur: Gen 12:1, 5 make Haran Abram's starting point, and the toponymic models for his relatives' names are in central Mesopotamia. This is Speiser's judgement, not a consensus.
claims.evidence: Speiser, Comment pp. 80–81 (read directly; quoted in §4.5). Labelled as Speiser's position: the cultural background of the patriarchal narratives "is intimately tied up with the Hurrians of Haran... rather than with the Sumerians and Babylonians in the south."

claims.claim: Harran (Ḥarranu, "a road") was a caravan centre on the Balikh, a centre of moon-god Sin worship (E-hul-hul), like Ur.
claims.evidence: Skinner (Harran = caravan centre, moon-god Sin, E-hul-hul, "Lord of Harran"); Ryle (Ḥarran, Assyrian Ḥarranu = "a road"; converging point of commercial routes; like Ur, a centre of moon-god Sin worship); Speiser, Note xi 31 (old and prominent city in Central Mesopotamia, left bank of the Balikh).

claims.claim: Sarai ("princess") and Milcah ("queen") may reflect Harran pantheon titles — Sarratu, the moon-goddess, consort of Sin, and Malkatu, a title of Ishtar among the deities worshipped in Harran. This is a proposal that raises questions about the Hebrew names' origin; it is not established.
claims.evidence: Skinner (Sarai = "princess", Milcah = "queen", possibly Harran pantheon titles Sarratu, Malkatu); Ryle (Sarratu = title of moon-goddess, consort of Sin; Malkatu = title of Ishtar — "raises questions about origin of Hebrew proper names Sarah and Milcah").

claims.claim: Terah's 205 years (MT) vs 145 (Sam): the Sam reading makes Abram's departure coincide with Terah's death and is followed by Stephen (Acts 7:4); the MT reading implies Abram left Haran at 75 while Terah was 145, i.e. before Terah's death (Augustine CD 16.15; Clarke). Which reading is original is unresolved.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:32; 12:4, read in full (the figures); Ryle (Sam 145; Stephen follows that tradition); K&D (same); Augustine CD 16.15 (read directly: Abram departed in Terah's 145th year, "not... after his father's death"); Clarke (Abram born when Terah was 130). See §7.5.

claims.claim: Abram's birth year: 11:26 states Terah was 70 when he begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Clarke infers Abram was born when Terah was 130 (Terah died 205; Abram left Haran at 75); Josephus gives Abram born 292 years after the deluge. The inferences are debated; the 11:26 statement is not.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:26, read in full; Clarke (Haran eldest, Abram youngest; born when Terah was 130); Josephus Ant. 1.6.5 (Abram born 292 years after the deluge; Arpachshad born 12 years after the deluge; Nahor 120 at Haran's birth). See §3.2.

claims.claim: Iscah (11:29) is identified with Sarai by rabbinical tradition (JFB; Augustine CD 16.12, "supposed to be the same as Sarah") and with Lot's wife by Ewald ("pure conjecture" per K&D).
claims.evidence: JFB (Sarai = Iscah, granddaughter of Terah by a second wife); Augustine CD 16.12 ("This Iscah is supposed to be the same as Sarah"); K&D (rabbinical notion irreconcilable with Gen 20:12; Ewald's hypothesis "pure conjecture").

claims.claim: The migration's motive is not stated in Genesis; later tradition (Judith 5:6–9, cited by Augustine CD 16.13) attributes religious persecution by the Chaldeans — the house of Terah would not follow the gods of their fathers and fled to Mesopotamia. Judith is deuterocanonical; the tradition is reception, not the biblical text.
claims.evidence: Augustine CD 16.13 (read directly, quoting Judith 5:6–9 via Achior); Ryle (later tradition, Judith 5:6–9, attributed religious causes; "no reason for migration assigned" in Genesis). Judith is not in the 66-book API — see rejected conn-R1.

claims.claim: "One lip and one speech" (11:1, śāp̄â ʾeḥāt) denotes a single common language. The passage's Hebrew vocabulary — śāp̄â "lip/speech", lāšôn "tongue", bālal "confuse", pûṣ "scatter", pālag "divide", šēm "name", migdāl "tower", ʿîr "city" — is the passage's own.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:1, read in full; BDB śāp̄â H8193 (sense 2 "language", Gen 11:1, 6, 7, 9), šēm H8034, migdāl H4026, ʿîr H5892, bālal H1101, pālag H6385, pûṣ H6327 (all read directly).

claims.claim: Correction to the task brief: the dispersion verb in Gen 10:18; 11:4, 8, 9 is pûṣ H6327 ("be dispersed, scattered"), not nāp̄aṣ. nāp̄aṣ is H5310 ("shatter" / "disperse"). The brief's "nāp̄aṣ H6327" conflates the two.
claims.evidence: BDB pûṣ H6327 (Niph'al Perfect 3pl nāp̄ōṣû Gen 10:18; Hiph'il wayyāp̄eṣ Gen 11:8) and nāp̄aṣ H5310, read directly via BibleHub.

claims.claim: Hebrew was held by Augustine (CD 16.11) to be the primitive language, preserved in Heber's house and exempt from the confusion as a punishment; the name "Hebrew" derives from Heber. Modern philology rejects Hebrew as the primitive language.
claims.evidence: Augustine CD 16.11 (read directly: "there was still the house of Heber in which the primitive language of the race survived... it was on this account thenceforth named Hebrew... it is fit to ascribe to the people of God an immunity from this punishment"); K&D, Ryle (Hebrew as primitive language "abandoned by modern philology").

claims.claim: Jubilees 8 gives the earliest elaborated three-lot division: Shem the middle of the earth, Ham the south, Japheth the north (8:12–29), with the climate theory attached (Japheth cold, Ham hot, Shem neither hot nor cold but blended, 8:30).
claims.evidence: Jubilees 8:12–30 (Charles translation, read in full via enocharchive).

claims.claim: The "three sons, three continents" scheme (Shem = Asia, Ham = Africa, Japheth = Europe) is a later tradition built on Jubilees 8, not stated in Genesis.
claims.evidence: Jubilees 8 (read directly — the source of the scheme); NS dossier §4.3 (the scheme is late); Josephus Ant. 1.6 (the ethnographic expansion without a continental systematisation).

claims.claim: Jubilees 10 adds to the builders' words "let us go up in it into heaven" (10:18, a storm-heaven purpose), gives the tower's dimensions (5,433 cubits and 2 palms high; 43 years building, 1645–1688 A.M., 10:21) and a mighty wind overthrowing it between Asshur and Babylon (10:26).
claims.evidence: Jubilees 10:18–27 (Charles translation, read in full via enocharchive and godrules.net).

claims.claim: Jubilees 8:7–11 dates the division of the earth to Peleg's birth (1567 A.M.) and the lot-division to the 33rd jubilee (1569 A.M.), with actual settlement deferred until the migration to Shinar (9:18); Canaan's seizure of Lebanon-to-Egypt (10:27–34) explains the land's name and justifies Israel's later possession.
claims.evidence: Jubilees 8:7–11; 9:18; 10:27–34 (Charles translation, read in full). The Free Library article (Jewish Bible Association, 2014) summarises the same material second-hand and is not cited as evidence.

claims.claim: Josephus (Ant. 1.4.2–3) makes Nimrod the instigator of the tower (revenge on God, a refuge against a second flood) and reports the Sibyl's account of the tower's overthrow by wind. Genesis 11 names no instigator.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 1.4.2–3 (Whiston, read in full via Gutenberg); KJV Gen 11:1–9, read in full (no instigator named); Calvin via JFB (the deluge-refuge theory as a "dream of their own brain").

claims.claim: Josephus (Ant. 1.6) gives the fullest ancient ethnographic expansion of the Table (Gomer → Galatians, Magog → Scythians, Madai → Medes, Javan → Ionia, etc.) and follows a 292-year Flood-to-Abram chronology, with Arpachshad born 12 years after the deluge.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 1.6.1–1.6.5 (Whiston, read in full via Gutenberg).

claims.claim: The dispersion is presented in Genesis as both judgement and the fulfilment of the creation mandate to fill the earth (cf. Gen 1:28; 9:1, 7, 19); the builders' refusal to scatter (11:4) is reversed by God's scattering (11:8–9).
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 11:4, 8–9; 9:18–19, read in full; Westermann (the dispersion motif already in the Flood's conclusion, 9:18–19, 10:25, same verb pûṣ). The theological reading is standard; the text states the reversal, not the mandate's fulfilment in so many words — hence Probable.

claims.claim: The nations multiplied faster than the languages: Augustine (CD 16.6) notes several African nations share one language, and that men "contrived to pass to the islands in ships" as the race increased.
claims.evidence: Augustine CD 16.6 (read directly: "the nations multiplied much more than the languages. For even in Africa we know several barbarous nations which have but one language").

connections.note: The bridge: "These three were the sons of Noah: and of them was the whole earth overspread." The Flood's conclusion points directly into the Table.
Noah's blessing of Shem ("Blessed be the LORD God of Shem") and Japheth ("God shall enlarge Japheth") — the oracles behind the Table's ordering (Shem last, the line traced forward).
The earlier tôlĕḏôt: Gen 11:10–26 resumes its pattern (ten generations vs nine; the same "lived... and begat" form).
Cain builds the first city ("he builded a city") — the city-building motif before Babel; the first city is built by a murderer, the second by a presumptuous generation.
The Nephilim/gibbôrîm, "mighty men which were of old, men of renown" — the parallel for Nimrod's gibbôr language (10:8–9).
Abram's call; "I will make of thee a great nation... and make thy name great" (12:2) answers Babel's "let us make us a name" (11:4) — God gives the name men tried to seize.
Abram departs Haran at 75 (12:4) — the Terah chronology problem (§7.5); "they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came" (12:5).
"I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees" — the only other occurrence of the phrase besides 11:28, 31.
"Aram-naharaim, unto the city of Nahor" — Nahor's city in the Harran region; the patriarchal family's continued tie to the north.
Amraphel king of Shinar — Shinar as a kingdom in the patriarchal narratives; the Table's Shinar (10:10) revisited.
Chronicles' retelling of the Table and the Shem genealogy — including the omission of Cainan at 1:24 (against the LXX's insertion in Gen 11:12).

"When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel" — the division of the nations as a divine act; Jubilees' lot-division (Jub 8–9) echoes it.

"Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods" — the family's pre-Abram religion; Augustine CD 16.12 cites it.
The remnant recovered "from Assyria, and from Egypt... and from Shinar" — Shinar named among the lands of dispersion.
"The language of Canaan" (śĕp̄at kĕnaʿan) — the language question: Hebrew as the tongue of Canaan (BDB śāp̄â H8193).
"I will punish Bel in Babylon" — the fall of the city Babel became; Gunkel cites Jer 50:37, 51:44 for Babel as world-market.
Javan, Tubal, and Meshech trading with Tyre — the Table's Japhethite names reused in prophecy (cf. Speiser on P's Japheth list known to Ezekiel).
Gog, Magog, Gomer, Togarmah — the Table's names in the Gog oracle (cf. Speiser: Magog = land of Gog; Gomer = Cimmerians). (Exact verses: Ezek 38:2, 6.)
"The land of Nimrod" (ʾereṣ nimrōd) — Assyria named for Nimrod; the only other biblical occurrence of his name besides Gen 10 and 1 Chr 1:10 (BDB H5248).
"I will turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD" — the prophetic reversal of Babel.
A house built for wickedness "in the land of Shinar" — Shinar as the destination of evil; the only other "land of Shinar" in the prophets besides Dan 1:2.

Nebuchadnezzar: "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?" — the pride of Babel's builder, answered by his humbling.
"Destroy, O Lord, and divide their tongues" (pālag) — the same root as Peleg's "division" (Gen 10:25) applied to tongues.
Pentecost: "every man heard them speak in his own language" — the converse of Babel (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 41 §16; Augustine, Sermon 271 — second-hand).
Stephen: Abram removed from Haran into Canaan "when his father was dead" — following the Sam (145-year Terah) tradition (§7.5).

"Hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation" — Paul's Areopagus summary of the Table and the Babel dispersion.
"Babylon the Great, the mother of harlots" — Babel's later reception as the archetype of the godless city.
"Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen" — the end of the city Babel became.
"I will go down now, and see" — the parallel for the LORD's "coming down" in Gen 11:5 (Ryle cites it for v. 5's anthropomorphism).
"Behold, the man is become as one of us" — the divine deliberation parallel to Gen 11:6–7 (Gunkel, Ryle cite Gen 3:22 alongside 6:1–4).
"I have made thee a great name" — God gives David the name Babel's builders tried to make for themselves (BDB šēm H8034, sense 2b).
"Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor" — the Caphtor origin of the Philistines, against the Casluhim origin of Gen 10:14.
